report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported by moderate-quality evidence, with important caveats**. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Kappelmann et al. (2018, *Molecular Psychiatry*), pooling randomized controlled trials of anti-cytokine drugs (mainly TNF-α and IL-6 inhibitors) used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and other chronic inflammatory conditions, found a statistically significant, moderate reduction in depressive symptoms compared with placebo (effect size ~0.4), even though these trials were not designed to test antidepressant effects (depression was a secondary outcome) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/, https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167). The effect appeared partly independent of improvements in physical disease activity, suggesting a direct effect on mood rather than simply relief from illness burden.

However, evidence in populations with primary depression rather than inflammatory disease is mixed. Raison et al.'s (2013, *JAMA Psychiatry*) RCT of the TNF antagonist infliximab in treatment-resistant depression found no overall benefit versus placebo, but a benefit emerged specifically among patients with elevated baseline inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP >5 mg/L) (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1356541). This indicates that anti-cytokine treatment's antidepressant effects may be limited to individuals with an inflammatory phenotype.

**Bottom line:** Anti-cytokine drugs do appear to reduce depressive symptoms in people with chronic inflammatory conditions, based on meta-analytic RCT data, but effects are modest, likely depend on baseline inflammation levels, and are not established as a general-purpose antidepressant treatment outside inflammatory disease contexts.
